Why Otters Hold Hands While Sleeping

Author: Jane Riverbank

Sea otters are among the few marine mammals that spend almost their entire lives in the water. To avoid drifting apart while they sleep, they often float on their backs in groups called rafts, and pairs frequently hold paws. This behaviour has fascinated researchers for decades because it combines social bonding with a very practical safety strategy.

The science of rafting

Rafts can contain anywhere from two to more than a thousand animals. Researchers at the Marine Institute found that the largest rafts form in sheltered kelp forests where the currents are weak and food is abundant, which suggests that location matters as much as company.

Otters also wrap themselves in kelp, anchoring their bodies to the sea floor. Mothers carry pups on their chests and teach them to groom, which keeps their dense fur waterproof and warm through the cold northern winters that would otherwise be deadly.

Key facts

  • Fur density: up to one million hairs per square inch
  • Diet: urchins, crabs and clams
  • Lifespan: 15 to 20 years
